claims.text: The initial material is a compositionally complex, homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with no pre-existing grain-boundary precipitates.
Prolonged exposure at 700–900 °C induces localized elemental segregation along grain boundaries in an initially single-phase HEA.
Slight differences in constituent-element diffusion rates drive the proposed grain-boundary segregation.
Diffusion of the constituent elements is sluggish but remains sufficient during prolonged thermal exposure to permit segregation.
Localized grain-boundary enrichment eventually exceeds the energetic threshold for precipitate nucleation.
Thermal exposure produces nanoscale precipitates in the HEA.
The thermally induced precipitates are specifically intergranular, incoherent, and intermetallic-like.
The intergranular precipitates are brittle and reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
Loss of grain-boundary cohesion causes emergent brittle behavior and reduced overall toughness.
The proposed HEA degradation differs from the rapid, large-scale precipitation expected in conventional alloys.
The unaged baseline is ductile and tough.
The unaged baseline has a uniform elemental distribution and lacks intergranular precipitates.
Aged specimens will have lower tensile ductility than otherwise identical unaged controls.
Aged specimens will have lower fracture toughness than otherwise identical unaged controls.
TEM and EDS will reveal nanoscale precipitates decorating grain boundaries after aging.
The proposed mechanism is active during extended service-like exposure at 700–900 °C.
The mechanism may not occur at lower temperatures because atomic mobility is insufficient.
The mechanism may not apply under conditions that instead promote rapid bulk precipitation.
A controlled comparison consists of aging specimens at about 800 °C for about 1000 hours in an inert atmosphere while retaining identically processed specimens in the unaged condition.
The hypothesis is falsified if aging produces neither a statistically significant toughness or ductility reduction nor detectable grain-boundary segregation or nanoscale precipitates.
